subject: chemistry
title: The halogens
key_idea: The halogens are diatomic molecules whose boiling points rise down the group as London forces strengthen. Their oxidising power falls down the group, so a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide. The hydrogen halides become less stable from HF to HI.

blocks.text: The halogens are the Group 17 elements. This section covers their structure, state, volatility, electronegativity and bond strength.

items: Each halogen exists as a **diatomic molecule**, X₂, held by one covalent bond.
The outer shell is s²p⁵. Halogen atoms gain one electron in many redox reactions to form 1− ions.

columns: Colour and state at room temperature

items: The molecules are simple molecular. Boiling overcomes **instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces** (London forces) between molecules, not the covalent bonds.
Down the group the molecules have more electrons, so the London forces are stronger.
More energy is needed to separate the molecules. Boiling points rise and volatility falls.
Melting points rise in the same way, which is why the state changes from gas (F₂, Cl₂) to liquid (Br₂) to solid (I₂).
Electronegativity **decreases** down the group.
Each atom has an extra shell and more shielding, so the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and attracted less.
The X–X bond gets weaker from Cl₂ to I₂: Cl–Cl 242, Br–Br 193 and I–I 151 kJ/mol.
The atoms get larger, so the shared pair is further from both nuclei and the overlap is poorer.
F–F (158 kJ/mol) is weaker than Cl–Cl. The F atoms are so small that the lone pairs on the two atoms repel.
Boiling point rises down the group because London forces get stronger.
Electronegativity falls down the group.
Bond strength falls from Cl₂ to I₂. F₂ is weaker than Cl₂.

blocks.text: The halogens are oxidising agents. This section covers how oxidising power changes and how displacement shows it.

items: Oxidising power **decreases** down the group.
A halogen atom takes in an electron to its outer shell. A smaller atom has less shielding and the electron is nearer the nucleus, so it is attracted more strongly.
Chlorine forms Cl⁻ more easily than bromine forms Br⁻ or iodine forms I⁻.

blocks.text: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from a solution of its halide.
Adding cyclohexane and shaking makes the colour clearer. The halogen is more soluble in the organic layer.

diagram.alt: A predictor. Pick a halogen added to a halide solution to see whether it reacts and the colours seen.
diagram.prompt: Pick a halogen and a halide solution.

items: Oxidising power falls down the group: Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide.
Solvent colours: bromine orange, iodine purple.

blocks.text: Halogens react with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides. This section covers how readily they form and how stable they are.

items: Fluorine reacts explosively with hydrogen, even in the dark and at low temperature.
Chlorine reacts explosively in sunlight, and bromine reacts only on heating.
Iodine reacts slowly and reversibly on heating.
The reactivity with hydrogen **decreases** down the group, in line with oxidising power.
The H–X bond formed is weaker down the group, so the reaction is less exothermic and less vigorous.

blocks.text: Thermal stability falls down the group because the H–X bond gets longer and weaker. HI breaks down on heating into H₂ and purple iodine vapour.

items: Reaction with hydrogen gets less vigorous down the group.
The H–X bond weakens from HF to HI, so thermal stability falls.

checks.q: Explain why the boiling points of the halogens increase from chlorine to iodine.
checks.a: The halogens are simple molecules, so London (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole) forces are overcome. Larger molecules have more electrons, so the forces are stronger and more energy is needed.

checks.q: Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution, followed by cyclohexane. Describe what is seen and write the ionic equation.
checks.a: The aqueous layer turns brown. The cyclohexane layer turns purple. Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂

checks.q: Explain why bromine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine.
checks.a: The bromine atom is larger and has more shielding. The incoming electron is further from the nucleus and attracted less, so Br₂ gains electrons less readily.

blocks.text: This part covers the halogen reactions as electron transfer, with oxidation numbers.

items: In each displacement, the halogen is **reduced**: its oxidation number falls from 0 to −1.
The halide is **oxidised**: its oxidation number rises from −1 to 0.
Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ and 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ are the two half-equations of the first displacement.
A full equation includes the spectator ion: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂.

blocks.text: The trend in reactivity follows how easily 1− ions form. This depends on attraction, atomic radius and shielding, as in the explanation above.
This part covers using the trend to predict fluorine, astatine and their compounds.

items: Fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent in the group and the most electronegative element. It displaces chlorine, bromine and iodine from their halides.
Fluorine is a pale yellow gas that reacts with water, and with almost everything.
Astatine is predicted to be a black solid at room temperature, with a boiling point above that of iodine.
Astatine would be the weakest oxidising agent of the group. It would not displace iodine from iodide.
HAt would be the least stable hydrogen halide and the strongest reducing agent among the hydrogen halides.
Silver astatide would be expected to be a precipitate that is even less soluble than AgI.
